transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I came in because I just... I can’t shake this feeling, this certainty really, that I’m being punished for what happened with my father. For letting him decline. I know people keep telling me that’s not true — my sister especially, she’ll show me the doctor’s notes and go over everything with me, like, “See, you did what you were supposed to do, you didn’t neglect him,” and I understand the words when she says them.

But it doesn’t change anything inside. It feels like some kind of judgment has already been passed on me, like it’s settled somewhere beyond what anyone can prove or disprove. I keep trying to reason with it, but it just sits there. That’s why I’m here.
Do you find yourself repeatedly doing anything to try and alleviate this feeling of being punished?

I don’t think so… not in a specific way, I mean. I keep going over it in my head, but I don’t know if that counts as “doing” something. It’s more like I’m trying to find the exact point where I failed him, or where I could have changed things, and then I’ll think maybe if I understand it clearly enough, the feeling will let up.

But I don’t have, like, a ritual or a thing I do that makes it better. Nothing reliably helps, really. Sometimes I’ll look back through what my sister has shown me or replay conversations, but it doesn’t actually take the punishment feeling away. It just keeps circling.
Are you having trouble doing your usual daily activities because of this feeling of being punished?

Yes. I mean, I was trying to tell myself I was still functioning because I still show up to work most days, but if I’m honest, I’m not doing my usual things the way I normally would.

At work, I’ve missed deadlines, which is not like me. I’m in human resources, so a lot of my job is keeping track of things, following through, having uncomfortable conversations when they need to happen. And lately I’ll just… avoid the difficult employee meetings. I’ll tell myself I need more time to prepare, or that I should wait until I’m steadier, but really I just can’t make myself walk into the room and hold it together. I feel too shaky inside, like this punishment thing is sitting right under my skin, and I’m afraid it’ll show or I’ll say the wrong thing.

And outside of work, I stopped going to my library volunteering. I used to be reliable with that. It wasn’t even something huge, but I cared about it, and I’d show up when I said I would. Now I just don’t. I keep thinking, “I can’t go there like this,” and then I don’t follow through. So yes, it’s definitely getting in the way.
Do you find yourself thinking about your father's decline and your perceived role in it at times when you're not trying to think about it?

Yes. Very much. It doesn’t stay where I put it, if that makes sense. I can be in the middle of something completely ordinary, like trying to answer an email at work or walking through the grocery store, and suddenly I’m back in it — thinking about one of my father’s appointments, whether I should have pushed harder, whether I missed something, whether I sounded impatient on the phone that one time.

And then it spreads. It’s not just the medical decisions, it’s every tense conversation with my relatives too. I’ll replay what I said, what they said, the tone of it, whether I was defending myself instead of focusing on him. I keep picking at it like there’s going to be one clear moment where I can say, “There, that’s when I failed.”

But it doesn’t end there. Once I start going over it, I end up feeling like… like I was selfish as a daughter. Like I made things about myself, or I didn’t give enough, or I only did the bare minimum even if other people say that isn’t true. And then somehow that turns into feeling useless everywhere else too, especially at work. If I miss something or put something off, it feels like proof that I’m not just failing in one part of my life — I’m failing as a person.

So yes, it comes up when I’m not trying to think about it. And when it does, I usually end up feeling like I deserve whatever happens because of it.
Have you been having trouble sleeping because of these thoughts about your father and feeling punished?

Yes. Sleep has been… really difficult. I can get into bed, but then I don’t actually fall asleep for a long time because my mind starts replaying everything. Phone calls with my father, phone calls about his care, decisions I made or didn’t make, whether I should have asked different questions, whether I missed some sign that seems obvious now.

It’s like once the house is quiet, there’s nothing to keep it pushed down. I’ll go over one conversation, then another, and I’ll think, “If I had said this differently,” or “If I had called sooner,” and then suddenly it’s hours later and I’m still awake.

And even when I do fall asleep, I’ve been waking up around 3 or 4 in the morning. Not just sort of stirring — I wake up with my chest tight, like something is already wrong before I’m even fully awake. Then the same thoughts are right there waiting for me. I try to tell myself I need to sleep because I have work, but that almost makes it worse, because then I’m watching the clock and thinking about how badly I’m going to do the next day.

Most mornings, I don’t really get back to sleep after that. I just lie there until it’s time to get up.
Do you feel compelled to perform any specific mental or physical acts in response to these thoughts about your father?

I’m not sure I’d call it a specific act, exactly. I don’t have, like… a set thing I have to do with my hands, or some routine I repeat a certain number of times, if that’s what you mean.

It’s more that I get stuck mentally. I’ll go over the same questions again and again — what I should have done, whether I caused harm by not doing enough, whether this is why I’m being punished. But I don’t know that I’m doing something in response to it so much as I can’t seem to stop turning it over.

Sometimes I’ll try to reason with myself, or I’ll sort of review the sequence of events in my head like I’m building a case, but it doesn’t really settle anything. I don’t feel relief afterward. It just loops. But no, I haven’t noticed any particular physical ritual or specific mental rule I have to follow.
Do you ever feel like these thoughts about being punished just pop into your head without you wanting to think about them?

Yes. They do. That’s actually a big part of why I came in, because it doesn’t feel like I’m choosing to think about it. I can be trying to focus on something else, and then all at once there it is again — this certainty that I’m being punished because I let my father decline.

And I know how that sounds. My sister has tried to talk me through it. She’s shown me the doctor’s notes, she’s reminded me of what was happening, what the doctors said, what I did do. She keeps telling me I did everything I reasonably could, that I didn’t cause it. And I can hear her saying it, and part of me understands the words, but it doesn’t really change the feeling.

It’s not just a worry, exactly. It feels like some kind of judgment has already been passed on me. Like the punishment is already in motion, and I’m just waiting for it to finish. Even when people give me evidence that I didn’t do something wrong, I still can’t shake it. It just comes back, like it knows better than they do.
Do you feel like you're unable to control these thoughts about your father and the feeling of being punished?

Yes… I mean, that’s the part that scares me. I can try to tell myself to stop, or I can try to go through the facts again, but it doesn’t really move. It’s not like a thought I can set aside and say, “Okay, that’s irrational, let’s move on.” It feels more solid than that.

I came in because I just can’t shake this certainty that I’m being punished for letting my father decline. And people keep trying to reassure me — especially my sister. She’ll remind me what the doctors said, she’ll point to things in the notes, she’ll say I did what I was supposed to do, that I didn’t abandon him or cause this. And I listen, I really do. I want to believe her.

But even when she lays it all out, it’s like it doesn’t reach the place where this feeling is coming from. It still feels like some judgment has already been made about me, and now I’m just living through the punishment for it. So yes, I feel like I can’t control it. I can distract myself for a little while maybe, but I can’t actually make it stop or make myself believe something different.
Do you feel like these thoughts about your father and being punished are intrusive, meaning they enter your mind without you wanting them to?

Yes… they come in when I’m not trying to think about them. I can be doing something completely ordinary, or trying to focus on work or a conversation, and then it just drops back into my mind — that I’m being punished for what happened with my father, for letting him decline.

But it’s not just like an annoying thought that interrupts me. It feels more… fixed than that. I came in because I can’t shake the certainty of it. Even when my sister sits with me and shows me the doctor’s notes, or tells me over and over that I did everything I was supposed to do, that I didn’t do anything wrong, it doesn’t really undo it. I can hear her, and I know she’s trying to help, but it still feels like some kind of judgment has already been passed on me.

So yes, they enter my mind without me wanting them to. But once they’re there, they don’t feel like just thoughts. They feel like something true that I’m being forced to face.
Do you feel an overwhelming urge to mentally or physically repeat certain actions in an attempt to counteract or make up for the perceived wrongs related to your father's decline?

I’m not sure I’d describe it that way, no. I mean… I do go over it in my head a lot, but I don’t think I have a specific thing I repeat to cancel it out, if that’s what you mean.

Like, I don’t have a ritual where I touch something a certain number of times or say a certain phrase or anything like that. And I don’t really have a routine that makes it feel “undone.” I might replay conversations, or think about what I should have done, or try to mentally argue with it for a while, but it doesn’t feel like an urge to perform an action so much as I get stuck in the feeling.

I guess I’m trying to answer carefully because I don’t want to say no too quickly if there’s something I’m missing. But as far as repeating actions to make up for it… no, I haven’t noticed that. It’s more like I feel it’s already true, and I can’t reason my way out of it.
Do you feel like you have to do something specific when these thoughts about your father and being punished come into your mind?

I don’t think there’s a specific thing I have to do, no. Not in the way you’re asking, I don’t think. When the thought comes in, I usually just… freeze with it for a while, or I start going back over everything in my head, but it’s not like I have to wash my hands, or check something, or repeat a sentence, or do some exact action to make it go away.

I might try to reassure myself, or I might think, “Okay, remember what my sister said, remember what the doctors said,” but it doesn’t feel like a required step that makes the punishment stop. It’s more like I’m trying to get relief and I can’t. I can sit there mentally reviewing it, almost like I’m looking for the one piece that will prove I’m not guilty, but I never actually find it in a way that settles anything.

So… no, I haven’t noticed a specific behavior or ritual. It’s more that once it’s in my mind, I get caught there. And I feel like I should somehow answer for it, but I don’t know what that “something” would even be.
Do you feel like you must perform a specific action when you think about your father's decline?

No… I don’t think I must perform a specific action. I know I’ve sort of said that already, but I want to be clear because the word “must” makes me think of something very exact, like I’d feel forced to do a particular thing or something bad would happen if I didn’t. And that’s not really how it is for me.

When I think about my father’s decline, I may get stuck there — I may sit and go over it, or feel like I should have done something differently, or try to make sense of it — but I don’t have a particular action I have to take. There isn’t a rule in my head like, “If you do this, it will fix it,” or “If you don’t do this, you’ll be punished more.” It’s more vague and heavy than that.

I might withdraw, or get quiet, or just keep replaying things mentally, but that doesn’t feel like performing an action. It feels more like I can’t get out from under the thought once it’s there. So… no, not a specific action. Just the feeling that I’m trapped with it.
Do you feel like these thoughts about being punished are a part of yourself, or do they feel like they're coming from outside of you?

It feels like it’s me, but not in a normal way, if that makes sense. I don’t hear it like it’s somebody standing outside me saying it. It’s not a voice in the room or anything like that. It’s in my own mind. But it doesn’t feel like just an ordinary worry either, because I can’t seem to step back from it.

I came in because I can’t shake this certainty that I’m being punished for letting my father decline. And I know how that sounds when I say it out loud — I know my sister has shown me the doctor’s notes, and she keeps telling me I did everything I could, that I wasn’t responsible in the way I keep thinking I was. I’ll even look at those things and try to take them in, like, “Okay, this is evidence, this should help.” But it doesn’t really land. Underneath it, it still feels like some judgment has already been passed on me.

So I guess the answer is… it feels like it’s inside me, but it also feels bigger than me. Like it’s not just a thought I’m choosing to have. It feels true, fixed, like I’m finally seeing what I deserve, even when other people are trying to tell me that isn’t what happened.
Do you feel like you have to repeat certain actions or behaviors in order to temporarily reduce your feelings of being punished?

I don’t think so… not in the way you mean. I don’t have a certain action I repeat to make the punished feeling go down, like doing something three times or checking something or saying a phrase over and over. I’ve tried to think about that because you’ve asked it a couple different ways, and I understand why you’re asking, but I really don’t think there’s a behavior like that.

What happens is more that I get stuck with the feeling. I may sit there and go over things in my head, but it isn’t like, “If I do this action, I’ll feel better for a little while.” There isn’t a clear relief cycle like that. Sometimes I might try to calm myself or remind myself of what other people have told me, but that’s more like grasping for something to hold onto, not a ritual or something I feel forced to repeat.

So… no, I haven’t noticed repeated actions or behaviors that temporarily reduce it. It’s more just that the feeling sits there, and I’m trying to endure it or reason with it, but it doesn’t really let up because I did some specific thing.
Do you feel like these thoughts about being punished are in line with your own beliefs and values?

I don’t know that they’re in line with what I would have said my beliefs and values were… not exactly. I mean, if you asked me in a normal moment what I believe, I would say people get sick, bodies fail, families do the best they can, and it isn’t fair or useful to blame one person for everything. I would say that to someone else. If a coworker came to me with this, or my sister, I’d probably tell her she was being cruel to herself.

But when it’s about my father, it doesn’t feel like just a belief I’m choosing. It feels more like… like a judgment that’s already there. I came in because I can’t shake this certainty that I’m being punished for letting him decline. And even when my sister shows me the doctor’s notes, or tells me I did everything right, or reminds me of what actually happened, it doesn’t really change the feeling. I can read it and understand the words, but underneath it I still feel like something has been decided about me.

So are they in line with my values? In one way, no — because I don’t want to believe in punishing people like that, and I don’t think I would judge anyone else that harshly. But in another way, it feels completely true when it’s aimed at me. Like I deserve it, like this is the consequence for what I failed to do. That’s the part I can’t seem to get around.
Do you feel like these thoughts about being punished are something you want to have, or are they unwelcome and something you wish you could stop thinking about?

No, I don’t want them. I really, really don’t. I know I keep saying it, but I came in because I can’t shake this certainty that I’m being punished for letting my father decline, and it’s exhausting. It isn’t like I sit there and decide, “This is what I believe and I want to keep thinking about it.” It’s more like it presses itself into everything, and even when I try to argue with it, it stays there.

I wish I could stop thinking about it. I wish I could believe my sister when she shows me the doctor’s notes or tells me I did everything right, because part of me understands what she’s saying. I can follow the logic of it. But it’s like the feeling underneath doesn’t move. It still feels like some judgment has already been passed on me, like I’m already guilty and this is what I deserve.

So yes, they’re unwelcome. I don’t want to keep living inside that thought. But at the same time, it doesn’t feel optional. It feels true in this horrible way, even when I’m trying not to believe it.
Do you feel like you must do something specific to try to make up for what happened with your father?

I don’t know if it’s one specific thing, like a task I can complete and then it would be made right. It’s not that clear. But I do feel like I should be doing something to make up for it all the time, if that makes sense.

Mostly I keep going back over everything — every appointment my father had, every time I should have pushed harder, every conversation with relatives where I got tense or defensive or tired. I replay it and think, why didn’t I notice more, why didn’t I say it better, why was I thinking about work or my own life when he was declining? And then it turns into this feeling that I was selfish. Like I was a selfish daughter, and now I have no right to expect things to go normally for me.

And it spills into work too. I’m in human resources, so I’m supposed to be someone who handles people’s problems, who pays attention, who helps. But I keep thinking, if I couldn’t even do right by my own father, then what am I doing helping anyone else? I feel useless there too, like I’m just pretending to be competent.

So I don’t have a specific act that feels like it would erase it. I just feel like I deserve whatever happens because I failed him. And I keep trying to review it, almost like if I can find the exact point where I went wrong, maybe I could understand what I’m supposed to pay back. But it never really ends.
Are these thoughts and feelings of being punished interfering with your relationships with friends or family?

Yes… it is. I mean, with family, I think I’m harder to be around now. My sister tries to reassure me, and I either shut down or I go over the same things again and again until I can tell she’s exhausted. And then I feel worse, because I think, well, now I’m making her carry this too.

With friends, I’ve pulled back. I don’t always answer messages, and if someone wants to make plans I keep thinking I won’t be able to act normal, or I’ll ruin the mood, or I’ll just sit there with this feeling hanging over me. So I say I’m busy, or I don’t respond quickly enough, and then it becomes harder to explain.

It’s also interfering outside of close relationships, if that counts. At work I’ve missed deadlines, which is not really like me, and I’ve avoided difficult employee meetings that I normally would handle. I keep thinking I’m not steady enough or not trustworthy enough to be the person in the room managing other people’s problems. And I stopped showing up for my library volunteering too. I used to be reliable there, and now I just… I can’t keep myself steady enough to follow through.

So yes, it’s affecting people. It’s not just something in my head that stays contained. It changes what I do, and then I feel guilty about that too.
Do you feel like these thoughts about being punished are consistent with your own sense of identity and self?

No… or, I don’t know. It’s hard to answer because part of me wants to say, “No, this isn’t me, I wasn’t always like this.” I didn’t used to see myself as someone who was living under some punishment. I used to think of myself as responsible, maybe too responsible sometimes, but not… condemned, I guess.

But now it feels like it has attached itself to who I am. Like when I think about myself, I don’t just think, “I’m someone whose father got sick,” I think, “I’m the person who let him decline.” And then the punishment part feels like it follows naturally from that, like it fits with this awful version of me that I can’t seem to disprove.

That’s what scares me, because even when my sister shows me the doctor’s notes or tells me I did everything right, even when I can understand the words she’s saying, it doesn’t really reach the part of me that feels judged. It still feels like some decision has already been made about me, like I’ve already been found guilty.

So I don’t want this to be my identity. I don’t want it to be how I understand myself. But right now it feels very bound up with me, like I can’t separate who I am from this certainty that I’m being punished for what happened with my father.
Do you feel guilty or ashamed about what happened with your father?

Yes. Very much. I feel guilty almost all the time, and ashamed too, though the shame is harder to say out loud.

I keep going back over every decision around my father’s appointments — whether I should have asked different questions, pushed harder, noticed something sooner, called someone else, gone with him more, argued less. It’s like my mind won’t let any of it rest. And then I think about the conversations with my relatives, the ones where I got tense or defensive or just tired, and I feel sick with myself. I think, what kind of daughter acts like that when her father is declining?

It always comes back to this feeling that I was selfish. Like I was thinking about my job, my schedule, my own stress, and somehow that means I failed him. And once I start there, it spreads. I don’t just feel guilty about one thing — I start feeling like the whole of me is wrong. Like I’m a selfish daughter, and even at work, like I’m useless there too. I work in human resources, I’m supposed to be helping people and paying attention to what they need, and I keep thinking, if I couldn’t do it for him, then who am I to sit there acting like I can help anyone?

So yes, I feel ashamed. I feel like I deserve whatever happens because of it. I know people tell me that isn’t fair, but it doesn’t feel unfair to me. It feels like something I earned.

patient.answer:
Yes. Very much. It doesn’t stay where I put it, if that makes sense. I can be in the middle of something completely ordinary, like trying to answer an email at work or walking through the grocery store, and suddenly I’m back in it — thinking about one of my father’s appointments, whether I should have pushed harder, whether I missed something, whether I sounded impatient on the phone that one time.

And then it spreads. It’s not just the medical decisions, it’s every tense conversation with my relatives too. I’ll replay what I said, what they said, the tone of it, whether I was defending myself instead of focusing on him. I keep picking at it like there’s going to be one clear moment where I can say, “There, that’s when I failed.”

But it doesn’t end there. Once I start going over it, I end up feeling like… like I was selfish as a daughter. Like I made things about myself, or I didn’t give enough, or I only did the bare minimum even if other people say that isn’t true. And then somehow that turns into feeling useless everywhere else too, especially at work. If I miss something or put something off, it feels like proof that I’m not just failing in one part of my life — I’m failing as a person.

So yes, it comes up when I’m not trying to think about it. And when it does, I usually end up feeling like I deserve whatever happens because of it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's feelings of guilt and punishment are interfering with their sleep

target_item.name: Sleep_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: I fall asleep late after replaying phone calls and care decisions, then I'm awake around 3 or 4 in the morning with my chest tight, unable to get back to sleep before work.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether thoughts about the father and feeling punished are causing trouble sleeping.

patient.answer:
Yes. Sleep has been… really difficult. I can get into bed, but then I don’t actually fall asleep for a long time because my mind starts replaying everything. Phone calls with my father, phone calls about his care, decisions I made or didn’t make, whether I should have asked different questions, whether I missed some sign that seems obvious now.

It’s like once the house is quiet, there’s nothing to keep it pushed down. I’ll go over one conversation, then another, and I’ll think, “If I had said this differently,” or “If I had called sooner,” and then suddenly it’s hours later and I’m still awake.

And even when I do fall asleep, I’ve been waking up around 3 or 4 in the morning. Not just sort of stirring — I wake up with my chest tight, like something is already wrong before I’m even fully awake. Then the same thoughts are right there waiting for me. I try to tell myself I need to sleep because I have work, but that almost makes it worse, because then I’m watching the clock and thinking about how badly I’m going to do the next day.

Most mornings, I don’t really get back to sleep after that. I just lie there until it’s time to get up.

But I don’t know that I’m doing something in response to it so much as I can’t seem to stop turning it over.

Sometimes I’ll try to reason with myself, or I’ll sort of review the sequence of events in my head like I’m building a case, but it doesn’t really settle anything. I don’t feel relief afterward. Yes. They do. That’s actually a big part of why I came in, because it doesn’t feel like I’m choosing to think about it. I can be trying to focus on something else, and then all at once there it is again — this certainty that I’m being punished because I let my father decline.

And I know how that sounds. My sister has tried to talk me through it. She’s shown me the doctor’s notes, she’s reminded me of what was happening, what the doctors said, what I did do. She keeps telling me I did everything I reasonably could, that I didn’t cause it. And I can hear her saying it, and part of me understands the words, but it doesn’t really change the feeling.

It’s not just a worry, exactly. It feels like some kind of judgment has already been passed on me. Like the punishment is already in motion, and I’m just waiting for it to finish. Even when people give me evidence that I didn’t do something wrong, I still can’t shake it. It just comes back, like it knows better than they do.

Yes… I mean, that’s the part that scares me. I can try to tell myself to stop, or I can try to go through the facts again, but it doesn’t really move. It’s not like a thought I can set aside and say, “Okay, that’s irrational, let’s move on.” It feels more solid than that.

I want to believe her.

But even when she lays it all out, it’s like it doesn’t reach the place where this feeling is coming from. It still feels like some judgment has already been made about me, and now I’m just living through the punishment for it. So yes, I feel like I can’t control it. I can distract myself for a little while maybe, but I can’t actually make it stop or make myself believe something different.

Even when my sister sits with me and shows me the doctor’s notes, or tells me over and over that I did everything I was supposed to do, that I didn’t do anything wrong, it doesn’t really undo it. I guess I’m trying to answer carefully because I don’t want to say no too quickly if there’s something I’m missing. But as far as repeating actions to make up for it… no, I haven’t noticed that. It’s more like I feel it’s already true, and I can’t reason my way out of it.

patient.answer:
No… I don’t think I must perform a specific action. When I think about my father’s decline, I may get stuck there — I may sit and go over it, or feel like I should have done something differently, or try to make sense of it — but I don’t have a particular action I have to take. There isn’t a rule in my head like, “If you do this, it will fix it,” or “If you don’t do this, you’ll be punished more.” It’s more vague and heavy than that.

I might withdraw, or get quiet, or just keep replaying things mentally, but that doesn’t feel like performing an action. It feels more like I can’t get out from under the thought once it’s there. So… no, not a specific action. Just the feeling that I’m trapped with it.

target_item.name: Delusions

It feels like it’s me, but not in a normal way, if that makes sense. I don’t hear it like it’s somebody standing outside me saying it. It’s not a voice in the room or anything like that. It’s in my own mind. But it doesn’t feel like just an ordinary worry either, because I can’t seem to step back from it.

I came in because I can’t shake this certainty that I’m being punished for letting my father decline. And I know how that sounds when I say it out loud — I know my sister has shown me the doctor’s notes, and she keeps telling me I did everything I could, that I wasn’t responsible in the way I keep thinking I was. I’ll even look at those things and try to take them in, like, “Okay, this is evidence, this should help.” But it doesn’t really land. Underneath it, it still feels like some judgment has already been passed on me.

So I guess the answer is… it feels like it’s inside me, but it also feels bigger than me. Like it’s not just a thought I’m choosing to have. It feels true, fixed, like I’m finally seeing what I deserve, even when other people are trying to tell me that isn’t what happened.

I don’t think so… not in the way you mean. So… no, I haven’t noticed repeated actions or behaviors that temporarily reduce it. It’s more just that the feeling sits there, and I’m trying to endure it or reason with it, but it doesn’t really let up because I did some specific thing.

target_item.name: Delusions

patient.answer:
I don’t know that they’re in line with what I would have said my beliefs and values were… not exactly. I mean, if you asked me in a normal moment what I believe, I would say people get sick, bodies fail, families do the best they can, and it isn’t fair or useful to blame one person for everything. I would say that to someone else. If a coworker came to me with this, or my sister, I’d probably tell her she was being cruel to herself.

But when it’s about my father, it doesn’t feel like just a belief I’m choosing. It feels more like… like a judgment that’s already there. I came in because I can’t shake this certainty that I’m being punished for letting him decline. And even when my sister shows me the doctor’s notes, or tells me I did everything right, or reminds me of what actually happened, it doesn’t really change the feeling. I can read it and understand the words, but underneath it I still feel like something has been decided about me.

So are they in line with my values? In one way, no — because I don’t want to believe in punishing people like that, and I don’t think I would judge anyone else that harshly. But in another way, it feels completely true when it’s aimed at me. Like I deserve it, like this is the consequence for what I failed to do. That’s the part I can’t seem to get around.

I wish I could stop thinking about it. I wish I could believe my sister when she shows me the doctor’s notes or tells me I did everything right, because part of me understands what she’s saying. I can follow the logic of it. But it’s like the feeling underneath doesn’t move. It still feels like some judgment has already been passed on me, like I’m already guilty and this is what I deserve.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of compulsions to perform specific acts
doctor.question: Do you feel like you must do something specific to try to make up for what happened with your father?

patient.answer:
I don’t know if it’s one specific thing, like a task I can complete and then it would be made right. It’s not that clear. But I do feel like I should be doing something to make up for it all the time, if that makes sense.

Mostly I keep going back over everything — every appointment my father had, every time I should have pushed harder, every conversation with relatives where I got tense or defensive or tired. I replay it and think, why didn’t I notice more, why didn’t I say it better, why was I thinking about work or my own life when he was declining? And then it turns into this feeling that I was selfish. Like I was a selfish daughter, and now I have no right to expect things to go normally for me.

And it spills into work too. I’m in human resources, so I’m supposed to be someone who handles people’s problems, who pays attention, who helps. But I keep thinking, if I couldn’t even do right by my own father, then what am I doing helping anyone else? I feel useless there too, like I’m just pretending to be competent.

So I don’t have a specific act that feels like it would erase it. I just feel like I deserve whatever happens because I failed him. And I keep trying to review it, almost like if I can find the exact point where I went wrong, maybe I could understand what I’m supposed to pay back. But it never really ends.

patient.answer:
Yes… it is. I mean, with family, I think I’m harder to be around now. My sister tries to reassure me, and I either shut down or I go over the same things again and again until I can tell she’s exhausted. And then I feel worse, because I think, well, now I’m making her carry this too.

With friends, I’ve pulled back. I don’t always answer messages, and if someone wants to make plans I keep thinking I won’t be able to act normal, or I’ll ruin the mood, or I’ll just sit there with this feeling hanging over me. So I say I’m busy, or I don’t respond quickly enough, and then it becomes harder to explain.

It’s also interfering outside of close relationships, if that counts. At work I’ve missed deadlines, which is not really like me, and I’ve avoided difficult employee meetings that I normally would handle. I keep thinking I’m not steady enough or not trustworthy enough to be the person in the room managing other people’s problems. And I stopped showing up for my library volunteering too. I used to be reliable there, and now I just… I can’t keep myself steady enough to follow through.

So yes, it’s affecting people. It’s not just something in my head that stays contained. It changes what I do, and then I feel guilty about that too.

No… or, I don’t know. It’s hard to answer because part of me wants to say, “No, this isn’t me, I wasn’t always like this.” I didn’t used to see myself as someone who was living under some punishment. I used to think of myself as responsible, maybe too responsible sometimes, but not… condemned, I guess.

But now it feels like it has attached itself to who I am. Like when I think about myself, I don’t just think, “I’m someone whose father got sick,” I think, “I’m the person who let him decline.” And then the punishment part feels like it follows naturally from that, like it fits with this awful version of me that I can’t seem to disprove.

That’s what scares me, because even when my sister shows me the doctor’s notes or tells me I did everything right, even when I can understand the words she’s saying, it doesn’t really reach the part of me that feels judged. It still feels like some decision has already been made about me, like I’ve already been found guilty.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of guilt or shame
doctor.question: Do you feel guilty or ashamed about what happened with your father?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep going over every decision about my father's appointments and every tense conversation with my relatives, and I end up feeling like I'm a selfish daughter and a useless employee who deserves whatever happens.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about feelings of guilt or shame related to what happened with the father.

patient.answer:
Yes. Very much. I feel guilty almost all the time, and ashamed too, though the shame is harder to say out loud.

I keep going back over every decision around my father’s appointments — whether I should have asked different questions, pushed harder, noticed something sooner, called someone else, gone with him more, argued less. It’s like my mind won’t let any of it rest. And then I think about the conversations with my relatives, the ones where I got tense or defensive or just tired, and I feel sick with myself. I think, what kind of daughter acts like that when her father is declining?

It always comes back to this feeling that I was selfish. Like I was thinking about my job, my schedule, my own stress, and somehow that means I failed him. And once I start there, it spreads. I don’t just feel guilty about one thing — I start feeling like the whole of me is wrong. Like I’m a selfish daughter, and even at work, like I’m useless there too. I work in human resources, I’m supposed to be helping people and paying attention to what they need, and I keep thinking, if I couldn’t do it for him, then who am I to sit there acting like I can help anyone?

So yes, I feel ashamed. I feel like I deserve whatever happens because of it. I know people tell me that isn’t fair, but it doesn’t feel unfair to me. It feels like something I earned.
